ukmt-jmo-2016-a01.title: Multiple of 10
ukmt-jmo-2016-a01.body:
One integer ends in $5$; the other ends in $4$ or $6$, so it is even. The product is a multiple of $5\times2=10$, and its square is a multiple of $100$. So the last two digits are $00$.

**Answer: 00**

ukmt-jmo-2016-a01.title: Example
ukmt-jmo-2016-a01.body:
Try $5\times6=30$, $30^2=900$; $14\times15=210$, $210^2=44100$. Always $00$, as the product is a multiple of $10$.

**Answer: 00**

ukmt-jmo-2016-a02.title: Angle chase
ukmt-jmo-2016-a02.body:
The two base angles of the large triangle are $35^\circ$, so its apex angle is $180-70=110^\circ$. Each outer small triangle has a $35^\circ$ angle at the base and a $35^\circ$ angle at the apex (isosceles), so its remaining angle is $110^\circ$; the middle triangle's base angles are therefore $180-110=70^\circ$ each. Then $x=180-70-70=40$.

**Answer: 40**

ukmt-jmo-2016-a02.title: Apex angle sum
ukmt-jmo-2016-a02.body:
The large triangle's apex angle is $110^\circ$ and it is made of the apex angles of the three small triangles: $35+x+35=110$, so $x=40$.

**Answer: 40**

ukmt-jmo-2016-a03.title: List the terms
ukmt-jmo-2016-a03.body:
The terms are $0,1,11,111,\ldots,111111111$ (the tenth term has nine $1$s). Adding: $1+11+111+\cdots+111111111=123456789$ (column by column: the units column has nine $1$s, the tens column eight, and so on).

**Answer: 123456789**

ukmt-jmo-2016-a04.title: Dissection
ukmt-jmo-2016-a04.body:
Cut the hexagon into three congruent parallelograms; each has area $16$. The shaded triangle is half of one parallelogram, so its area is $8$ m$^2$.

**Answer: 8 m$^2$**

ukmt-jmo-2016-a04.title: Small triangles
ukmt-jmo-2016-a04.body:
Divide the hexagon into $6$ equilateral triangles of area $8$ each. The shaded triangle has the same area as one of them (same base and height), so $8$.

**Answer: 8 m$^2$**

ukmt-jmo-2016-a05.title: Fold step by step
ukmt-jmo-2016-a05.body:
The area is $600$, which halves each fold: $300,150,75$, so three folds. The shorter line of symmetry halves the longer side: $30\times20\to15\times20\to15\times10\to7.5\times10$. Perimeter $=2(7.5+10)=35$ cm.

**Answer: 35 cm**

ukmt-jmo-2016-a07.title: Find the number
ukmt-jmo-2016-a07.body:
The integer is a multiple of $\text{lcm}(15,21)=105=3\cdot5\cdot7$. $105$ has exactly $2^3=8$ factors, and any larger multiple has more, so the integer is $105$. The factors are $1,3,5,7,15,21,35,105$ with sum $192$.

**Answer: 192**

ukmt-jmo-2016-a08.title: Equation
ukmt-jmo-2016-a08.body:
In $x$ years: $32+x=(4+x)+(1+x)=5+2x$, so $x=27$ and Julie will be $59$ (Megan $31$, Zoey $28$).

**Answer: 59**

ukmt-jmo-2016-a08.title: Gap closes
ukmt-jmo-2016-a08.body:
The sum of the daughters' ages is $5$ and grows by $2$ a year, Julie's age grows by $1$ a year, so the gap $32-5=27$ closes by $1$ a year. After $27$ years Julie is $59$.

**Answer: 59**

ukmt-jmo-2016-a09.title: Add the arcs
ukmt-jmo-2016-a09.body:
The perimeter of one region is a third of the big circle plus two semicircles of radius $9$: $\frac13\cdot2\pi\cdot18+2\cdot\frac12\cdot2\pi\cdot9=12\pi+18\pi=30\pi$ cm.

**Answer: $30\pi$ cm**

ukmt-jmo-2016-a10.title: Equal triangles
ukmt-jmo-2016-a10.body:
The $14$ small triangles with a side on the divided diagonal have equal bases and the same height, hence equal areas, and they fill the rectangle (area $63$). The shaded region is $6$ of them: $\frac{6}{14}\times63=27$ cm$^2$.

**Answer: 27 cm$^2$**

ukmt-jmo-2016-b01.title: Algebra
ukmt-jmo-2016-b01.body:
Let the other two angles be $a$ and $b$. The third is $30+\frac{a+b}2$, so $a+b+30+\frac{a+b}{2}=180$, giving $a+b=100$. The third angle is $80^\circ$. Each of $a,b$ is at least $1$, so the largest is $99$ (triangle $1^\circ,80^\circ,99^\circ$).

**Answer: 99**

ukmt-jmo-2016-b02.title: Equations
ukmt-jmo-2016-b02.body:
Touching externally means the distance between centres is the sum of radii. With radii $a,b,c$ at $A,B,C$ and $AB=13$, $BC=16$, $AC=20$: $a+b=13$, $b+c=16$, $a+c=20$. Adding: $a+b+c=24.5$. Hence $c=24.5-13=11.5$, $a=24.5-16=8.5$, $b=24.5-20=4.5$.

So the radii are $4.5$, $8.5$ and $11.5$ cm.

ukmt-jmo-2016-b03.title: Edge cubes
ukmt-jmo-2016-b03.body:
A small cube touches $3$ others at a corner, $4$ along an edge (not at a corner), $5$ in the middle of a face and $6$ inside. So the cubes touching four others are the non-corner cubes on the $12$ edges: $168\div12=14$ per edge. Each edge then has $14+2=16$ cubes, so the large cube has $16^3=4096$ small cubes.

**Answer: 4096**

ukmt-jmo-2016-b04.title: Angle chase
ukmt-jmo-2016-b04.body:
Triangle $EBC$ is equilateral, so $\angle BCE=60^\circ$. Since $ED\parallel AB$, $\angle ABC=\angle BCE=60^\circ$ (alternate angles).

Drop perpendiculars from $D$ and $C$ to $AB$ meeting it at $H$ and $G$. Then $DH=CG$ (distance between parallels) and $DA=CB$, so the right triangles $DAH$ and $CBG$ are congruent (RHS) and $\angle DAH=\angle CBG=60^\circ$. Hence $\angle DAB=60^\circ$ and, as $DAF$ is a straight line, $\angle BAF=180^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ$.

In isosceles triangle $AFB$ ($AF=AB$): $\angle FBA=\frac12(180^\circ-120^\circ)=30^\circ$.

Therefore $\angle FBC=\angle FBA+\angle ABC=30^\circ+60^\circ=90^\circ$. ∎

ukmt-jmo-2016-b05.title: Build up the counts
ukmt-jmo-2016-b05.body:
A shortest path uses only moves up or right (5 of each). Write in each cell the number of shortest paths from $S$ to it: each cell not on the left or bottom edge is reached from the left or from below, so its number is the sum of those two (cells in the hole count $0$). The first row and column are all $1$; filling in the board around the central hole gives $52$ at $F$.

**Answer: 52**

ukmt-jmo-2016-b05.title: Subtract paths through the hole
ukmt-jmo-2016-b05.body:
Without the hole there are $\binom{10}{5}=252$ shortest paths. Counting those that avoid the $2\times2$ hole by the same addition rule gives $52$.

**Answer: 52**

ukmt-jmo-2016-b06.title: Construction by induction
ukmt-jmo-2016-b06.body:
$n=1$: $1+2+3=6$ would need each group to sum to $2$, impossible ($3>2$).

$n=2$: $\{1,6\},\{2,5\},\{3,4\}$ each sum to $7$.

$n=3$: sum $45$, groups $\{1,2,3,4,5\},\{6,9\},\{7,8\}$ each $15$.

Suppose the integers $1,\ldots,3n$ can be split into three equal-sum groups. Going to $3(n+2)$ we add the six numbers $3n+1,\ldots,3n+6$. Pair them as $(3n+1,3n+6)$, $(3n+2,3n+5)$, $(3n+3,3n+4)$; each pair sums to $6n+7$, and we add one pair to each group. The sums stay equal. So from $n=2$ we get all even $n\ge2$, and from $n=3$ all odd $n\ge3$.

Thus it is possible exactly when $n>1$. ∎
